newsitem.title: UK: Grain group sees another bumper wheat crop in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Grain group sees another bumper wheat crop in 1997.

text.p: Farmers around the world, having watched the price of wheat plummet, will curtail sowings and shift to other crops but a leading grain monitor on Tuesday still projected a larger harvest in 1997.
The International Grains Council (IGC) -- which comprises importers and exporters -- forecast a wheat harvest of 580 million tonnes in 1997, up five million from this year.
Growers would switch to alternative crops now that the price of wheat has plunged by some 40 percent from its peak of over $200 a tonne.
But reaction would be limited in the northern hemisphere, where sowings were mostly completed before the downturn began.
With production increasing, the IGC expected the recovery in stocks from recent 20-year lows to continue next season from this year's estimated 102 million tonnes.
The moderate build-up in stocks would weigh on prices.
But in the longer term, as governments increasingly withdraw from grain markets and publicly-held stocks drop, prices would again fluctuate sharply.

"The relationship between stocks and prices has not been proportionate, with the maximum price effect recently occurring with a relatively small increase or decrease from existing stock levels," said Bill de Maria, IGC's assistant executive director.
"This may become more frequent as the world wheat industry learns to function with a smaller overall margin between supply and demand," he added.
In its first projection of the 1997 wheat harvest, the IGC expected a recovery in output in central and eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union and the United States.
China and the European Union (EU) might sustain their high level of production, but Australia and Argentina were unlikely to see a repeat of this season's bumper crops.
"Lower prices for wheat might...be expected to lead to a reduction in sowings," it said.

But this year's output from the two southern hemisphere countries would continue to pressure prices in the coming months. The IGC further raised the 1996 production estimates for Argentina and Australia to 15.5 million and 21 million tonnes respectively.
In Canada, where the bulk of wheat is spring sown, production decisions for next year would be strongly influenced by price levels for other crops.

The wheat area in the EU could increase with the reduction in compulsory land set-aside from 10 percent to five percent and a preference for high-yielding varieties, but the record average yield of 1996 might not be repeated, the IGC said.
Conditions were reported to be better than last year in the United States, but the sown area could be slightly lower.
India would remain vulnerable to moisture shortages as only a third of the sown area is irrigated. Crops have benefited strongly from a succession of good monsoons in recent years.
Russia'a output could continue to decline and its import requirements would largely depend on whether the livestock industry regains its strength.

The IGC raised its estimate for world wheat production in 1996 by two million tonnes to 575 million, mainly due to better crops in Australia and Argentina. But it trimmed the figure for end-season stocks by two million tonnes to 102 million.

It also revised up its estimate for coarse grains output -- mainly maize, barley and oats -- to a record 884 million tonnes from the previous forecast of 875 million after reports of a larger U.S. maize crop, now seen at 235 million tonnes.
It projected end-season coarse grain stocks at a sharply higher 114 million tonnes from last month's estimate of 105 million.
